d/dx x^{n} = nx^{n−1}.title: Power rule
d/dx x^{n} = nx^{n−1}.about: To differentiate a power of x, bring the exponent down in front and lower it by one. It is the most-used rule in calculus and, with the sum rule, differentiates any polynomial term by term.
assumptions: n is any real constant (integer, fraction or negative), not a function of x
For non-integer n, x > 0 so that x^{n} is defined (x ≠ 0 when n < 1)
n = 0 gives d/dx 1 = 0: constants have zero slope
vars: the variable you differentiate with respect to

example.problem: Find the slope of y = x^{3} at x = 2.

d/dx e^{x} = e^{x}.title: Derivative of e^{x}
d/dx e^{x} = e^{x}.about: The natural exponential is its own derivative: the slope of e^{x} at any point equals its height. That is what makes e the natural base and why e^{x} solves y′ = y.
assumptions: With an inner function use the chain rule: d/dx e^{kx} = k e^{kx}
vars: the variable you differentiate with respect to

example.problem: A quantity grows as N(t) = 100 e^{0.05t}. How fast is it growing at t = 10?

d/dx b^{x} = b^{x} ln b.title: Derivative of an exponential with base b
d/dx b^{x} = b^{x} ln b.about: Write b^{x} = e^{x ln b} and use the chain rule: the derivative is the function itself times ln b. Bases above e grow faster than their own value; bases below e grow slower.
assumptions: For 0 < b < 1, ln b < 0 and the function decreases
vars: the variable you differentiate with respect to

example.problem: Find the slope of y = 2^{x} at x = 3.

d/dx ln x = 1/x.title: Derivative of the natural log
d/dx ln x = 1/x.about: The slope of ln x is the reciprocal of x: steep near zero and flattening as x grows. It is why logarithmic differentiation works and why ∫ 1/x dx is a log.
assumptions: x > 0, where ln x is defined
For x < 0, d/dx ln|x| = 1/x as well
With an inner function: d/dx ln u = u′/u
vars: the positive argument of the log

example.problem: Find the slope of y = ln x at x = 4.

d/dx log_{b}x = 1/(x ln b).title: Derivative of a log with base b
d/dx log_{b}x = 1/(x ln b).about: Change the base to natural logs, log_{b}x = ln x/ln b, and differentiate: the slope is 1/x scaled by 1/ln b. For base 10 the factor is 1/ln 10 ≈ 0.4343.
vars: the positive argument of the log

example.problem: Find the slope of y = log_{10}x at x = 5.

d/dx sin x = cos x.title: Derivative of sine
d/dx sin x = cos x.about: The slope of the sine curve at x is cos x: steepest (slope ±1) where sine crosses zero, flat at its peaks and troughs. Used for velocity in simple harmonic motion and anywhere oscillations appear.
assumptions: x is in radians; in degrees an extra factor π/180 appears
With an inner function: d/dx sin(kx) = k cos(kx)
related: ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C

example.problem: A mass moves as x(t) = 0.2 sin(3t) m. Find its velocity at t = 0.5 s.

d/dx cos x = −sin x.title: Derivative of cosine
d/dx cos x = −sin x.about: The slope of the cosine curve at x is −sin x: cosine falls through the first half-turn, where sine is positive. Differentiating cos twice gives −cos, the signature of simple harmonic motion.

example.problem: Find the slope of y = cos x at x = π/6.

d/dx tan x = sec^{2}x.title: Derivative of tangent
d/dx tan x = sec^{2}x.about: Differentiate sin x/cos x with the quotient rule: (cos^{2}x + sin^{2}x)/cos^{2}x = 1/cos^{2}x. The tangent is always increasing between its asymptotes, and steeper the closer it gets to them.

example.problem: Find the slope of y = tan x at x = π/4.

d/dx cot x = −csc^{2}x.title: Derivative of cotangent
d/dx cot x = −csc^{2}x.about: Differentiate cos x/sin x with the quotient rule: (−sin^{2}x − cos^{2}x)/sin^{2}x = −1/sin^{2}x. The cotangent is always decreasing between its asymptotes.

example.problem: Find the slope of y = cot x at x = π/6.

d/dx sec x = sec x tan x.title: Derivative of secant
d/dx sec x = sec x tan x.about: Write sec x = (cos x)^{−1} and use the chain rule: −(cos x)^{−2}(−sin x) = sin x/cos^{2}x = sec x tan x.
related: ∫ sec x tan x dx = sec x + C
d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x

example.problem: Find the slope of y = sec x at x = π/3.
steps: At x = π/3: sec = 2, tan = √3, so 2√3

d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x.title: Derivative of cosecant
d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x.about: Write csc x = (sin x)^{−1} and use the chain rule: −(sin x)^{−2} cos x = −csc x cot x.
related: ∫ csc x cot x dx = −csc x + C
d/dx sec x = sec x tan x

example.problem: Find the slope of y = csc x at x = π/6.
steps: At x = π/6: csc = 2, cot = √3, so −2√3

d/dx arcsin x = 1/√(1 − x^{2}).title: Derivative of arcsine
d/dx arcsin x = 1/√(1 − x^{2}).about: If y = arcsin x then sin y = x; differentiate implicitly, cos y · y′ = 1, and cos y = √(1 − x^{2}). It appears whenever you differentiate an angle found from a ratio.
assumptions: −1 < x < 1 (the slope is infinite at x = ±1)
arcsin returns angles in [−π/2, π/2], in radians

example.problem: Find the slope of y = arcsin x at x = 0.6.

d/dx arccos x = −1/√(1 − x^{2}).title: Derivative of arccosine
d/dx arccos x = −1/√(1 − x^{2}).about: arccos x = π/2 − arcsin x, so its slope is the negative of arcsine's. arccos is decreasing on its whole domain.
assumptions: arccos returns angles in [0, π], in radians

example.problem: Find the slope of y = arccos x at x = 0.6.

d/dx arctan x = 1/(1 + x^{2}).title: Derivative of arctangent
d/dx arctan x = 1/(1 + x^{2}).about: If y = arctan x then tan y = x; differentiate implicitly, sec^{2}y · y′ = 1, and sec^{2}y = 1 + x^{2}. Defined for every x, it is the derivative behind ∫ 1/(1 + x^{2}) dx.
assumptions: arctan returns angles in (−π/2, π/2), in radians

example.problem: Find the slope of y = arctan x at x = 2.

(fg)′ = f′g + fg′.title: Product rule
(fg)′ = f′g + fg′.about: The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives: each factor takes a turn being differentiated while the other is held. Use it whenever two functions of x are multiplied.
assumptions: f and g are both differentiable at the point
Extends to three factors: (fgh)′ = f′gh + fg′h + fgh′

example.problem: Differentiate y = x^{2} sin x and evaluate at x = π/2.
steps: f = x^{2}, f′ = 2x; g = sin x, g′ = cos x
y′ = 2x sin x + x^{2} cos x

(fg)′ = f′g + fg′.try: d/dx x^2 sin(x rad) at x=pi/2

(f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g^{2}.title: Quotient rule
(f/g)′ = (f′g − fg′)/g^{2}.about: Differentiates one function divided by another: bottom times derivative of the top, minus top times derivative of the bottom, over the bottom squared. The order in the numerator matters.
assumptions: f and g are differentiable at the point

example.problem: Differentiate y = x/(x^{2} + 1) at x = 2.

f(g(x))′ = f′(g(x)) g′(x).title: Chain rule
f(g(x))′ = f′(g(x)) g′(x).about: For a function inside another, differentiate the outside (leaving the inside alone), then multiply by the derivative of the inside. In Leibniz form, dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx.
assumptions: g is differentiable at x and f is differentiable at g(x)
Chains of any length multiply: each layer contributes its own derivative

example.problem: Differentiate y = (3x + 1)^{5} at x = 0.

∫ x^{n} dx = x^{n+1}/(n + 1) + C.title: Power rule for integrals
∫ x^{n} dx = x^{n+1}/(n + 1) + C.about: Reverse the power rule: raise the exponent by one and divide by the new exponent. Integrates any polynomial term by term.
assumptions: n constant; for non-integer n, x > 0
Add C for an indefinite integral; drop it between limits

∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C.title: Integral of 1/x
∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C.about: The one power the power rule misses: x^{−1} integrates to a log. The absolute value lets it work for negative x too.
assumptions: x ≠ 0; a definite integral must not cross x = 0
On x > 0 alone you can write ln x + C

∫ e^{x} dx = e^{x} + C.title: Integral of e^{x}
∫ e^{x} dx = e^{x} + C.about: Since e^{x} is its own derivative, it is its own antiderivative too. With a linear inner function, ∫ e^{kx} dx = e^{kx}/k + C.

∫ b^{x} dx = b^{x}/ln b + C.title: Integral of an exponential with base b
∫ b^{x} dx = b^{x}/ln b + C.about: Reverse of d/dx b^{x} = b^{x} ln b: divide by ln b.

∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C.title: Integral of sine
∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C.about: Since d/dx cos x = −sin x, the antiderivative of sin x is −cos x. Over a whole period the integral is zero; over a half-period it is 2.
assumptions: With kx inside: ∫ sin kx dx = −cos(kx)/k + C
related: ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C

example.problem: Find the area under one arch of y = sin x, from 0 to π.

∫ cos x dx = sin x + C.title: Integral of cosine
∫ cos x dx = sin x + C.about: Since d/dx sin x = cos x, the antiderivative of cos x is sin x.
assumptions: With kx inside: ∫ cos kx dx = sin(kx)/k + C

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π/6} cos x dx.

∫ sec^{2}x dx = tan x + C.title: Integral of sec²x
∫ sec^{2}x dx = tan x + C.about: Reverse of d/dx tan x = sec^{2}x. Paired with 1 + tan^{2}x = sec^{2}x it also integrates tan^{2}x = sec^{2}x − 1.
assumptions: The interval must not contain π/2 + kπ

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π/4} sec^{2}x dx.

∫ csc^{2}x dx = −cot x + C.title: Integral of csc²x
assumptions: The interval must not contain kπ

example.problem: Find ∫_{π/4}^{π/2} csc^{2}x dx.

∫ sec x tan x dx = sec x + C.title: Integral of sec x tan x
∫ sec x tan x dx = sec x + C.about: Reverse of d/dx sec x = sec x tan x.
assumptions: The interval must not contain π/2 + kπ
related: d/dx sec x = sec x tan x

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π/3} sec x tan x dx.

∫ csc x cot x dx = −csc x + C.title: Integral of csc x cot x
∫ csc x cot x dx = −csc x + C.about: Reverse of d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x.
assumptions: The interval must not contain kπ
related: d/dx csc x = −csc x cot x

example.problem: Find ∫_{π/6}^{π/2} csc x cot x dx.

∫ csc x cot x dx = −csc x + C.try: integral(cos(x rad)/sin(x rad)^2, x, pi/6, pi/2)

∫ tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C.title: Integral of tangent
∫ tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C.about: Write tan x = sin x/cos x and substitute u = cos x: −∫ du/u = −ln|cos x| = ln|sec x|.
assumptions: The interval must not contain π/2 + kπ, where tan blows up
related: ∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π/3} tan x dx.

∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C.title: Integral of cotangent
∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C.about: Write cot x = cos x/sin x and substitute u = sin x: ∫ du/u = ln|sin x|.
assumptions: The interval must not contain kπ
related: ∫ tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C

example.problem: Find ∫_{π/6}^{π/2} cot x dx.

∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C.try: integral(cos(x rad)/sin(x rad), x, pi/6, pi/2)

∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C.title: Integral of secant
∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C.about: Multiply top and bottom by sec x + tan x; the numerator becomes the derivative of the denominator, giving a log. It turns up in Mercator's map projection and in trig-substitution integrals.
assumptions: The interval must not contain π/2 + kπ
related: ∫ csc x dx = −ln|csc x + cot x| + C

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π/4} sec x dx.
steps: [ln|sec x + tan x|] from 0 to π/4

∫ csc x dx = −ln|csc x + cot x| + C.title: Integral of cosecant
∫ csc x dx = −ln|csc x + cot x| + C.about: Multiply top and bottom by csc x + cot x; the numerator is minus the derivative of the denominator, giving a negative log. An equal form is ln|tan(x/2)|.
assumptions: The interval must not contain kπ
related: ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C

example.problem: Find ∫_{π/2}^{2π/3} csc x dx.

∫ sin^{2}x dx = x/2 − sin 2x/4 + C.title: Integral of sin²x
∫ sin^{2}x dx = x/2 − sin 2x/4 + C.about: Use the power-reducing identity sin^{2}x = (1 − cos 2x)/2 and integrate each term. Over a whole period the average of sin^{2} is 1/2, which is behind RMS values.

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π} sin^{2}x dx.

∫ cos^{2}x dx = x/2 + sin 2x/4 + C.title: Integral of cos²x
∫ cos^{2}x dx = x/2 + sin 2x/4 + C.about: Use cos^{2}x = (1 + cos 2x)/2 and integrate each term.

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{π/4} cos^{2}x dx.

∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C.title: Integral of ln x
∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C.about: Integrate by parts with u = ln x, dv = dx: x ln x − ∫ x · (1/x) dx = x ln x − x.
related: ∫ log_{b}x dx = (x ln x − x)/ln b + C

example.problem: Find ∫_{1}^{e} ln x dx.
steps: [x ln x − x] from 1 to e

∫ log_{b}x dx = (x ln x − x)/ln b + C.title: Integral of a log with base b
∫ log_{b}x dx = (x ln x − x)/ln b + C.about: Change base, log_{b}x = ln x/ln b, then use ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x.
related: ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + C

∫ 1/√(1 − x^{2}) dx = arcsin x + C.title: Integral giving arcsine
∫ 1/√(1 − x^{2}) dx = arcsin x + C.about: Reverse of d/dx arcsin x. The substitution x = sin θ turns the root into cos θ and the integral into θ.
assumptions: The answer is an angle in radians

∫ 1/(1 + x^{2}) dx = arctan x + C.title: Integral giving arctangent
∫ 1/(1 + x^{2}) dx = arctan x + C.about: Reverse of d/dx arctan x. Over the whole real line the integral is π, a classic improper integral.
assumptions: The answer is an angle in radians

∫ 1/√(a^{2} − x^{2}) dx = arcsin(x/a) +.title: Integral of 1/√(a² − x²)
∫ 1/√(a^{2} − x^{2}) dx = arcsin(x/a) +.about: Substitute x = a sin θ: dx = a cos θ dθ and the root is a cos θ, leaving ∫ dθ.

∫ 1/(a^{2} + x^{2}) dx = (1/a) arctan(x/.title: Integral of 1/(a² + x²)
∫ 1/(a^{2} + x^{2}) dx = (1/a) arctan(x/.about: Substitute x = a tan θ: dx = a sec^{2}θ dθ and a^{2} + x^{2} = a^{2} sec^{2}θ, leaving (1/a)∫ dθ. Completing the square brings many quadratics to this form.

∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du.title: Integration by parts
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du.about: The product rule run backwards. Pick u to get simpler when differentiated (logs, powers of x) and dv to be easy to integrate (exponentials, trig). The LIATE order (Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential) suggests which factor is u.
assumptions: u and v are differentiable on the interval
With limits: ∫_{a}^{b} u dv = [uv]_{a}^{b} − ∫_{a}^{b} v du
It may need repeating, or loop back to the original integral and be solved for it

example.problem: Find ∫_{0}^{1} x e^{x} dx.
steps: u = x, dv = e^{x} dx → du = dx, v = e^{x}
∫ x e^{x} dx = x e^{x} − ∫ e^{x} dx = (x − 1)e^{x}

x = (−b ± √(b^{2} − 4ac))/(2a).title: Quadratic formula
x = (−b ± √(b^{2} − 4ac))/(2a).about: Solves ax^{2} + bx + c = 0 for any coefficients, found by completing the square. The ± gives the two roots.
assumptions: The discriminant b^{2} − 4ac decides the roots: > 0 two real, = 0 one repeated, < 0 two complex

Δ = b^{2} − 4ac.title: Discriminant
Δ = b^{2} − 4ac.about: The part under the root in the quadratic formula. Its sign tells you, without solving, whether a quadratic has two real roots, one repeated root or none (two complex roots).
assumptions: Real coefficients for the sign test to mean real versus complex

example.problem: How many real roots does x^{2} + 4x + 5 = 0 have?

x = −b/(2a).title: Vertex of a parabola
x = −b/(2a).about: The x of the turning point of y = ax^{2} + bx + c, halfway between the roots. It is a minimum when a > 0 and a maximum when a < 0; put it back in to get the extreme value.
vars: x-coordinate of the vertex (axis of symmetry)

example.problem: A ball's height is h = −4.9t^{2} + 19.6t + 1 m. When is it highest, and how high?

y = a(x − h)^{2} + k.title: Vertex form of a parabola
y = a(x − h)^{2} + k.about: A parabola written to show its vertex (h, k) directly. a sets the width and whether it opens up (a > 0) or down (a < 0). Complete the square to get here from ax^{2} + bx + c.

example.problem: Write y = 2x^{2} − 8x + 3 in vertex form.

y = m x + b.title: Slope-intercept form of a line
y = m x + b.about: A straight line with slope m (rise over run) that crosses the y-axis at b.
assumptions: Not for vertical lines (x = constant), whose slope is undefined

example.problem: A line passes through (1, 3) and (4, 9). Find its equation.

y − y_{1} = m(x − x_{1}).title: Point-slope form of a line
y − y_{1} = m(x − x_{1}).about: The line with slope m through the point (x_{1}, y_{1}). Quickest when you know a point and a slope, as with a tangent line.
vars: a known point on the line

example.problem: Find the tangent line to y = x^{2} at x = 3, and its y at x = 3.5.

m_{1} m_{2} = −1.title: Perpendicular slopes
m_{1} m_{2} = −1.about: Two lines are perpendicular when their slopes are negative reciprocals.
assumptions: Neither line is vertical or horizontal (a horizontal line, slope 0, is perpendicular to a vertical one)

example.problem: Find the slope of a line perpendicular to y = 2/3 x + 1.

(x − h)^{2} + (y − k)^{2} = r^{2}.title: Circle
(x − h)^{2} + (y − k)^{2} = r^{2}.about: Every point at distance r from the centre (h, k), from the distance formula. With h = k = 0 it is x^{2} + y^{2} = r^{2}.

example.problem: Find the radius of the circle centred at (1, −2) that passes through (4, 2).

x^{2}/a^{2} + y^{2}/b^{2} = 1.title: Ellipse
x^{2}/a^{2} + y^{2}/b^{2} = 1.about: An ellipse centred at the origin with semi-axes a along x and b along y. Each focus sits at distance c = √(a^{2} − b^{2}) from the centre when a > b. Shifted to (h, k): replace x with x − h and y with y − k.

example.problem: Find the foci of x^{2}/25 + y^{2}/9 = 1.

x^{2}/a^{2} − y^{2}/b^{2} = 1.title: Hyperbola
x^{2}/a^{2} − y^{2}/b^{2} = 1.about: A hyperbola opening left and right, with vertices at (±a, 0) and asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x. Foci are at (±c, 0) with c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}.
assumptions: Swap the signs (y^{2} term positive) for one opening up and down
vars: distance from centre to each vertex

example.problem: Find the foci of x^{2}/9 − y^{2}/16 = 1.

y^{2} = 4 p x.title: Parabola (focus form)
y^{2} = 4 p x.about: A parabola opening along +x with its vertex at the origin, focus at (p, 0) and directrix x = −p. Every point is as far from the focus as from the directrix, which is why dishes and headlights use it.
assumptions: p ≠ 0; p < 0 opens to the left
x^{2} = 4py is the same parabola opening up

example.problem: A dish follows y^{2} = 12x. Where is the focus?

a_{n} = a_{1} + (n − 1) d.title: Arithmetic sequence
a_{n} = a_{1} + (n − 1) d.about: Each term adds the same common difference d to the last, so the n-th term is the first plus n − 1 steps of d. Linear growth: seat rows, straight-line depreciation, evenly spaced readings.
assumptions: d is constant; it may be negative or zero

example.problem: A theatre's first row has 20 seats and each row has 3 more. How many seats are in row 15?

S_{n} = n(a_{1} + a_{n})/2.title: Sum of an arithmetic sequence
S_{n} = n(a_{1} + a_{n})/2.about: The number of terms times the average of the first and last. Gauss's trick: pair the first with the last, the second with the second-last, and every pair has the same sum.
vars: sum of the first n terms

example.problem: Add the odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … + 39.

a_{n} = a_{1} r^{n−1}.title: Geometric sequence
a_{n} = a_{1} r^{n−1}.about: Each term multiplies the last by the same common ratio r. Exponential growth or decay: compound interest, bounces, half-lives.
assumptions: r is constant and nonzero; r < 0 alternates the sign

example.problem: A ball dropped from 2 m rebounds to 70% of its height each bounce. How high is the 5th rebound?

S_{n} = a_{1}(1 − r^{n})/(1 − r).title: Sum of a geometric sequence
S_{n} = a_{1}(1 − r^{n})/(1 − r).about: Multiply the sum by r and subtract: almost every term cancels, leaving a_{1}(1 − r^{n}). Used for savings plans, loan payments and finite echoes.
assumptions: r ≠ 1 (for r = 1 the sum is n a_{1})
vars: sum of the first n terms

example.problem: Find 3 + 6 + 12 + … to 8 terms.

S = a_{1}/(1 − r).title: Infinite geometric series
S = a_{1}/(1 − r).about: Let n → ∞ in the finite sum: when |r| < 1, r^{n} → 0 and the sum settles to a_{1}/(1 − r). It is how 0.999… = 1 and how a repeating decimal becomes a fraction.

example.problem: A ball is dropped from 10 m and each bounce rises to 60% of the previous height. How far does it travel in all?

log_{b}(x) = ln(x)/ln(b).title: Change of base
log_{b}(x) = ln(x)/ln(b).about: Any log can be written with natural logs (or base 10). Use it when a calculator only has ln and log.

example.problem: Find log_{2}(50).

log_{b}(xy) = log_{b}(x) + log_{b}(y).title: Log of a product
log_{b}(xy) = log_{b}(x) + log_{b}(y).about: Logs turn multiplication into addition, because exponents add when powers multiply. This is what decibels and slide rules exploit.

log_{b}(x^{n}) = n log_{b}(x).title: Log of a power
log_{b}(x^{n}) = n log_{b}(x).about: An exponent inside a log comes out in front as a factor. It is the step that solves equations with the unknown in the exponent.

example.problem: Solve 3^{x} = 20.
steps: Take ln of both sides: x ln 3 = ln 20

0° ‖ 0 ‖ 0 ‖ 1 ‖ 0.title: Unit circle at 0°
0° ‖ 0 ‖ 0 ‖ 1 ‖ 0.about: The point at 0° (0 rad) on the unit circle is (cos, sin) = (1, 0), on the positive x-axis. tan = sin/cos = 0.
assumptions: Angles in degrees here equal the radians column (180° = π rad)
vars: the angle, in degrees or radians

example.problem: A 2 m arm pivots at the origin and points at 0° from the +x axis. Where is its tip?

30° ‖ π/6 ‖ 1/2 ‖ √3/2 ‖ √3/3.title: Unit circle at 30°
30° ‖ π/6 ‖ 1/2 ‖ √3/2 ‖ √3/3.about: The point at 30° (π/6 rad) on the unit circle is (cos, sin) = (√3/2, 1/2), in quadrant I. tan = sin/cos = √3/3.
assumptions: Angles in degrees here equal the radians column (180° = π rad)
vars: the angle, in degrees or radians

example.problem: A 2 m arm pivots at the origin and points at 30° from the +x axis. Where is its tip?

45° ‖ π/4 ‖ √2/2 ‖ √2/2 ‖ 1.title: Unit circle at 45°
45° ‖ π/4 ‖ √2/2 ‖ √2/2 ‖ 1.about: The point at 45° (π/4 rad) on the unit circle is (cos, sin) = (√2/2, √2/2), in quadrant I. tan = sin/cos = 1.
assumptions: Angles in degrees here equal the radians column (180° = π rad)
vars: the angle, in degrees or radians

example.problem: A 2 m arm pivots at the origin and points at 45° from the +x axis. Where is its tip?

60° ‖ π/3 ‖ √3/2 ‖ 1/2 ‖ √3.title: Unit circle at 60°
60° ‖ π/3 ‖ √3/2 ‖ 1/2 ‖ √3.about: The point at 60° (π/3 rad) on the unit circle is (cos, sin) = (1/2, √3/2), in quadrant I. tan = sin/cos = √3.
assumptions: Angles in degrees here equal the radians column (180° = π rad)
vars: the angle, in degrees or radians

f(x) = Σ_{n=0}^{∞} f^{(n)}(a) (x − a)^{n.title: Taylor series
f(x) = Σ_{n=0}^{∞} f^{(n)}(a) (x − a)^{n.about: Rebuilds a smooth function near x = a from its value and all its derivatives there. Cutting it off after a few terms gives a polynomial approximation, which is how calculators and linearisations work.
assumptions: f has derivatives of every order at a
The series converges only within its radius of convergence, and must also converge to f (true for e^{x}, sin, cos and most functions met in practice)
A truncated series is accurate near a; the error grows with |x − a|
vars: n-th derivative of f at a
the point where the series is evaluated

example.problem: Estimate √4.1 with the first three terms of the Taylor series of √x about a = 4.

e^{x} = Σ x^{n}/n! = 1 + x + x^{2}/2! +.title: Series for e^{x}
e^{x} = Σ x^{n}/n! = 1 + x + x^{2}/2! +.about: Every derivative of e^{x} is e^{x}, which is 1 at 0, so each coefficient is 1/n!. The factorials make it converge fast for any x.
assumptions: Converges for every real (and complex) x
For large |x| you need more terms
vars: the point where the series is evaluated
related: e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x
Euler's formula, from the three series

example.problem: Estimate e^{0.5} with five terms.

sin x = Σ (−1)^{n} x^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)! =.title: Series for sin x
sin x = Σ (−1)^{n} x^{2n+1}/(2n + 1)! =.about: Odd powers only, with alternating signs, because sine is odd and its derivatives cycle sin, cos, −sin, −cos. The first term gives the small-angle approximation sin x ≈ x.
assumptions: For an alternating series the error is smaller than the first term left out

example.problem: Estimate sin(0.5 rad) with three terms.

cos x = Σ (−1)^{n} x^{2n}/(2n)! = 1 − x^.title: Series for cos x
cos x = Σ (−1)^{n} x^{2n}/(2n)! = 1 − x^.about: Even powers only, with alternating signs, because cosine is even. Its first two terms give cos x ≈ 1 − x^{2}/2, used for pendulums and small deflections.

example.problem: Estimate cos(0.5 rad) with three terms.

sinh x = x + x^{3}/3! + x^{5}/5! + ….title: Series for sinh x
sinh x = x + x^{3}/3! + x^{5}/5! + ….about: The odd half of the e^{x} series: sinh x = (e^{x} − e^{−x})/2. Like sin x but with every sign positive.
vars: the point where the series is evaluated

example.problem: Estimate sinh 1 with three terms.

cosh x = 1 + x^{2}/2! + x^{4}/4! + ….title: Series for cosh x
cosh x = 1 + x^{2}/2! + x^{4}/4! + ….about: The even half of the e^{x} series: cosh x = (e^{x} + e^{−x})/2. A hanging cable (catenary) follows cosh, and its first two terms show it is nearly a parabola near the bottom.
vars: the point where the series is evaluated

example.problem: Estimate cosh 1 with three terms.

1/(1 − x) = Σ x^{n} = 1 + x + x^{2} + x^.title: Geometric series
1/(1 − x) = Σ x^{n} = 1 + x + x^{2} + x^.about: The infinite geometric series with first term 1 and ratio x. Substituting, differentiating or integrating it produces many other series (ln(1 + x), arctan x).
related: the same sum with first term a_{1}

example.problem: Check the series at x = 0.2 by summing it.

ln(1 + x) = x − x^{2}/2 + x^{3}/3 − ….title: Series for ln(1 + x)
ln(1 + x) = x − x^{2}/2 + x^{3}/3 − ….about: Integrate 1/(1 + t) = 1 − t + t^{2} − … from 0 to x. Near zero ln(1 + x) ≈ x, the rule behind small percentage changes and continuous compounding.
assumptions: −1 < x ≤ 1 (at x = 1 it converges slowly, to ln 2)

example.problem: Estimate ln 1.1 with three terms.

tan^{−1} x = x − x^{3}/3 + x^{5}/5 − ….title: Series for arctan x
tan^{−1} x = x − x^{3}/3 + x^{5}/5 − ….about: Integrate 1/(1 + t^{2}) = 1 − t^{2} + t^{4} − … from 0 to x. At x = 1 it gives the Leibniz series π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − …
assumptions: The answer is an angle in radians

example.problem: Estimate arctan 0.2 with three terms.

(1 + x)^{a} = 1 + ax + a(a − 1)x^{2}/2!.title: Binomial series
(1 + x)^{a} = 1 + ax + a(a − 1)x^{2}/2!.about: Newton's extension of the binomial theorem to any exponent a. Its first two terms, (1 + x)^{a} ≈ 1 + ax, are the workhorse approximation for roots and small corrections (relativity, error propagation).
assumptions: |x| < 1 when a is not a non-negative integer
For a = 0, 1, 2, … it stops after a + 1 terms and holds for every x

example.problem: Estimate √1.06 = (1 + 0.06)^{1/2} with three terms.

∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, ∂f/∂z).title: Gradient
∇f = (∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, ∂f/∂z).about: A vector of the partial derivatives of a scalar field. It points in the direction of steepest increase, its length is that steepest rate, and it is perpendicular to level surfaces. Heat flows along −∇T.
assumptions: f has partial derivatives at the point (continuous ones for the directional-derivative formula)
Cartesian coordinates; cylindrical and spherical forms differ
related: directional derivative along unit vector u

example.problem: f = x^{2}y + yz. Find ∇f and its magnitude at (1, 2, 3).

∇ · F = ∂F_{x}/∂x + ∂F_{y}/∂y + ∂F_{z}/∂.title: Divergence
∇ · F = ∂F_{x}/∂x + ∂F_{y}/∂y + ∂F_{z}/∂.about: A scalar measuring how much a vector field spreads out from a point: positive at a source, negative at a sink, zero for an incompressible flow.

∇ × F = (∂F_{z}/∂y − ∂F_{y}/∂z, ∂F_{x}/∂.title: Curl
∇ × F = (∂F_{z}/∂y − ∂F_{y}/∂z, ∂F_{x}/∂.about: A vector measuring how a field swirls around a point: its direction is the axis of rotation (right-hand rule) and its size is twice the local angular velocity of a fluid. Zero curl means the field is irrotational.
assumptions: Cartesian coordinates; it is the determinant of (i, j, k; ∂/∂x, ∂/∂y, ∂/∂z; F_{x}, F_{y}, F_{z})

example.problem: A fluid spins as a rigid body, v = (−ωy, ωx, 0) with ω = 3 rad/s. Find ∇ × v.

∇^{2} f = ∂^{2}f/∂x^{2} + ∂^{2}f/∂y^{2}.title: Laplacian
∇^{2} f = ∂^{2}f/∂x^{2} + ∂^{2}f/∂y^{2}.about: The divergence of the gradient: it compares f at a point with its average nearby. It appears in the heat, wave, Laplace and Schrödinger equations; ∇^{2}f = 0 describes steady temperature and electrostatic potential in empty space.

∇ × (∇f) = 0.title: Curl of a gradient is zero
∇ × (∇f) = 0.about: A gradient field never swirls, because mixed partial derivatives are equal (∂^{2}f/∂x∂y = ∂^{2}f/∂y∂x). So a conservative force, F = −∇U, always has zero curl.
assumptions: f has continuous second partial derivatives
The converse (zero curl means a gradient) needs a simply connected region

example.problem: Check it for f = x^{2}y: find the z-component of ∇ × ∇f.

∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.title: Divergence of a curl is zero
∇ · (∇ × F) = 0.about: A curl field has no sources or sinks, again because mixed partials cancel. It is why ∇ · B = 0 lets the magnetic field be written B = ∇ × A.
assumptions: F has continuous second partial derivatives

example.problem: Check it for F = (yz, x^{2}, 0).

∫_{C} ∇f · dr = f(b) − f(a).title: Gradient theorem
∫_{C} ∇f · dr = f(b) − f(a).about: The fundamental theorem of calculus for line integrals: integrating a gradient along any path depends only on the endpoints. Work done by a conservative force is minus the change in potential energy.
assumptions: f is differentiable with a continuous gradient on a region containing C
C is a piecewise-smooth curve from a to b
vars: a path from point a to point b

example.problem: F = ∇f with f = xy + z^{2}. Find ∫ F · dr from (0, 0, 0) to (2, 3, 1) along any path.

∮_{C} (P dx + Q dy) = ∬_{D} (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/.title: Green's theorem
∮_{C} (P dx + Q dy) = ∬_{D} (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/.about: Turns a line integral around a closed plane curve into a double integral of the 'circulation density' over the region inside. With P = −y/2, Q = x/2 it gives the area of a region from its boundary (the planimeter).
assumptions: C is a simple closed, piecewise-smooth curve traversed counter-clockwise, enclosing D
P and Q have continuous partial derivatives on D (no holes or singularities inside)
vars: components of a plane vector field (P, Q)

example.problem: Find ∮ (−y dx + x dy) around the circle of radius 2.

∮_{C} F · dr = ∬_{S} (∇ × F) · dS.title: Stokes' theorem
∮_{C} F · dr = ∬_{S} (∇ × F) · dS.about: The circulation of a field around a closed loop equals the flux of its curl through any surface bounded by the loop. It is the math behind Ampère's and Faraday's laws in integral form.
assumptions: S is a piecewise-smooth oriented surface with boundary C
C is oriented by the right-hand rule with S's normal
F has continuous partial derivatives on S

example.problem: A field F = (−y, x, 0) has curl (0, 0, 2). Find its circulation around a horizontal circle of radius 0.5 m.
steps: Flux of the curl through the disc: 2 × π(0.5)^{2}

∯_{S} F · dS = ∭_{V} (∇ · F) dV.title: Divergence theorem
∯_{S} F · dS = ∭_{V} (∇ · F) dV.about: The net flux out of a closed surface equals the total divergence (sources minus sinks) inside. It turns conservation laws and Gauss's law between integral and differential form.
assumptions: S is a closed, piecewise-smooth surface bounding V, normal pointing outward
F has continuous partial derivatives throughout V

example.problem: Find the outward flux of F = (x, y, z) through a sphere of radius 2.
